claims.claim: Norton abolished Congress by decree, and it was ignored
claims.quote: Norton issued numerous decrees on matters of state, including a decree on October 12, 1859, to formally abolish the United States Congress. ... Norton's orders were ignored by Army and Congress.

claims.claim: Joshua Norton declared himself Emperor of the United States in September 1859
claims.quote: Norton proclaimed himself "Emperor of these United States" in September 1859, a role he played for the rest of his life.

claims.claim: He held the role for twenty years
claims.quote: and thus began Norton's whimsical 20-year "reign" over the United States

claims.claim: The uniform was a secondhand gift from the Army
claims.quote: He wore an elaborate blue uniform with gold-plated epaulettes, at some time given to him secondhand by officers of the United States Army post at the Presidio of San Francisco.

claims.claim: Officers at the Presidio of San Francisco gave him the blue coat and gold-plated epaulettes
claims.quote: at some time given to him secondhand by officers of the United States Army post at the Presidio of San Francisco

claims.claim: He added a feathered beaver hat
claims.quote: He embellished that with a variety of accoutrements, including a beaver hat decorated with a peacock or ostrich feathers and a rosette, a walking stick, and an umbrella.

claims.claim: The 1870 census listed his occupation as "Emperor"
claims.quote: The 1870 U.S. census lists Joshua Norton as 50 years old and residing at 624 Commercial Street, with his occupation listed as "Emperor."

claims.claim: The census recorded him at 624 Commercial Street, aged 50, and noted he was insane
claims.quote: The 1870 U.S. census lists Joshua Norton as 50 years old and residing at 624 Commercial Street, with his occupation listed as "Emperor." It also notes that he was insane.

claims.claim: He had no formal political power at all
claims.quote: Norton had no formal political power but was treated deferentially in San Francisco and elsewhere in California

claims.claim: The velocipede photograph dates from 1869
claims.quote: FILE: velocipede.jpg ... Date: 1869

claims.claim: He printed his own money and restaurants accepted it
claims.quote: Norton issued his own money in the form of scrip, or promissory notes, which were accepted from him by some restaurants in San Francisco.

claims.claim: The notes ran from fifty cents to ten dollars
claims.quote: The notes came in denominations between fifty cents and ten dollars

claims.claim: The few surviving notes sell for more than $10,000 at auction
claims.quote: the few surviving ones are collector's items that routinely sell for more than $10,000 at auction

claims.claim: The edict image is a printed edict of Norton I dated 22 May 1879
claims.quote: Given under our hand and seal, this twenty-second day of May, A. D., 1879.   NORTON I. [SEAL.]

claims.claim: The two dogs were never Norton's
claims.quote: Caricaturist Edward Jump often depicted Norton with two noted stray dogs named Bummer and Lazarus, giving rise to the rumor that the dogs were Norton's pets. There is no evidence to support this.

claims.claim: Caricaturist Edward Jump repeatedly drew Norton with strays Bummer and Lazarus
claims.quote: Caricaturist Edward Jump often depicted Norton with two noted stray dogs named Bummer and Lazarus

claims.claim: Norton was a bankrupt rice speculator
claims.quote: Norton's failed effort to corner the rice market in December 1852 set in motion a cascade of events ... that forced him to declare bankruptcy in August 1856.

claims.claim: He received free ferry passes and free meals
claims.quote: Norton received free ferry and train passage and a variety of favors, such as help with rent and free meals, from well-placed friends and sympathizers.

claims.claim: Police saluted him
claims.quote: Police officers of San Francisco thereafter saluted Norton as he passed in the street.

claims.claim: No birth record survives for Norton
claims.quote: There is not a birth record for Norton, but he was most likely born in Deptford.

claims.claim: His obituaries disagreed about his year of birth
claims.quote: Obituaries published in 1880, following Norton's death, offered conflicting information about his date of birth.

claims.claim: On 17 September 1859 Norton hand-delivered a letter to the Daily Evening Bulletin declaring himself "Emperor of these United States"
claims.quote: Two months later, on September 17, 1859, Norton hand-delivered the following letter declaring himself "Emperor of these United States" to the offices of the Bulletin

claims.claim: The paper printed it for humorous effect
claims.quote: The paper printed the letter in that evening's edition, for humorous effect

claims.claim: His decrees abolished the US Congress in October 1859
claims.quote: including a decree on October 12, 1859, to formally abolish the United States Congress

claims.claim: He ordered Major-General Scott to clear the halls of Congress with a suitable force
claims.quote: we do hereby Order and Direct Major-General Scott, the Commander-in-Chief of our Armies, immediately upon receipt of this, our Decree, to proceed with a suitable force and clear the Halls of Congress.

claims.claim: The Army ignored him
claims.quote: Norton's orders were ignored by Army and Congress.

claims.claim: In 1869 he abolished the Democratic and Republican parties
claims.quote: In a proclamation dated August 12, 1869, and published in the San Francisco Daily Herald, he declared the abolition of the Democratic and Republican parties

claims.claim: He wrote to Queen Victoria proposing marriage and she never replied
claims.quote: Norton wrote many letters to Queen Victoria, including a suggestion that they marry to strengthen ties between their nations. That proved futile because the queen never responded.

claims.claim: He received help with rent
claims.quote: Norton received free ferry and train passage and a variety of favors, such as help with rent and free meals, from well-placed friends and sympathizers.

claims.claim: A private security guard arrested him in 1867 to commit him for a mental disorder
claims.quote: Special officer Armand Barbier was part of a local auxiliary force whose members were called "policemen," although they were private security guards paid by neighborhood residents and business owners. He arrested Norton in 1867 to commit him to involuntary treatment for a mental disorder.

claims.claim: The newspapers turned on the police over the arrest
claims.quote: The arrest outraged many citizens and sparked scathing editorials in the newspapers

claims.claim: The police chief released him and apologised, and Norton pardoned the guard
claims.quote: Police Chief Patrick Crowley ordered Norton released and issued a formal apology on behalf of the police force, and Norton granted an Imperial Pardon to Barbier.

claims.claim: He died on a wet pavement on 8 January 1880
claims.quote: On the reeking pavement, in the darkness of a moonless night, under the dripping rain ... Norton I, by the grace of God, Emperor of the United States and Protector of Mexico, departed this life.

claims.claim: He had five or six dollars in change on him when he died
claims.quote: Five or six dollars in small change was found on his person

claims.claim: Some 10,000 people viewed the body
claims.quote: the San Francisco Chronicle reported, under the headline "Le Roi Est Mort," that some 10,000 people had come to view the emperor's body in advance of the 2 p.m. funeral

claims.claim: The "Frisco" fine decree has no traceable source
claims.quote: although evidence is elusive for the authorship, date, or source of this decree

claims.claim: Local papers printed fake proclamations under his name for years
claims.quote: local newspapers, notably the Daily Alta California, began to print fictitious decrees. It is believed that newspaper editors themselves drafted the fake proclamations to suit their own agendas.

claims.claim: He named the Black-owned Pacific Appeal his "imperial organ" in 1870
claims.quote: in December 1870 Norton named the black-owned and -operated Pacific Appeal as his "imperial organ."
